groups.text: A payment service builds its objects by hand in main, each one after the objects its constructor needs.
A dependency injection container does that for you.
Here is the one you'll build.
At start-up it finds the components, orders them, and builds each singleton once.
Timed and Retry methods get a proxy.
A generator can write the same wiring at build time, for a faster start.
Lesson one, in Java, wires classes by reflection.
The scanner loads each class without initializing it, so no static initializer runs.
It never guesses a constructor, and it skips the synthetic ones Kotlin adds.
A depth-first walk orders the graph, and names any cycle at start-up.
Each singleton gets a cell with double-checked locking: one instance, even when eight threads ask at once.
Lesson two, in Kotlin, adds Timed and Retry.
Interceptors run around each call, with Timed outside Retry.
A component with an interface gets a J D K proxy around its target.
A class without one gets a Byte Buddy subclass.
A subclass can't override what Kotlin leaves final, so the container refuses that at start-up.
Lesson three, in Java, measures it and makes it start fast.
Per call, J M H counts two hundred eight bytes for a J D K proxy, and one hundred sixty for a subclass.
At start-up, the app loads two thousand two hundred seven classes.
A class histogram and a heap dump show what the container keeps alive.
Then a generator runs the same graph at build time, and writes a holder class per singleton.
The start drops to nine hundred ninety-one classes.
It writes Java.
In Kotlin, an object is the same kind of holder.
AppCDS and the A O T cache then archive what is left.
One rule holds throughout: never guess, never skip in silence.
What the classes alone can tell, the container checks before the first call, at start-up, or in the build.
